Below is a draft essay. Revise it so that it reads as if a US grade 8 student wrote it in class for a timed writing test. Keep the position it argues and keep it at about 487 words. The file must contain only the revised essay.

Draft:

When people face a hard decision, they often reach out to more than one person for advice. At first this might seem like a way to put off choosing, but it usually leads to better decisions. Asking several people gives a person a wider range of knowledge, helps cancel out any one adviser's bias, and lets them test their own thinking before they commit.

The first benefit is that different people know different things. Nobody has experience with everything. Imagine a high school senior trying to pick between a state university and a community college. Her guidance counselor can explain transfer credits and admission rates. Her older cousin, who went to community college first, can describe what it actually felt like to save money while friends moved away. A parent can talk honestly about what the family can afford. Each person holds one piece of the picture, and only by talking to all of them does she see the whole thing. If she had asked just one, she would have made her choice with important facts missing.

Second, every adviser carries some bias, even when they mean well. A coach may push a talented athlete to focus on sports because the team needs him. A music teacher may tell the same student to practice more piano. Neither is lying, but each sees the student through their own interests. When the student hears both opinions, he can notice where they pull in different directions and ask himself what he wants. Several opinions work almost like a balance. A single strong voice can tip a person toward a choice that serves someone else, while many voices help them find the middle and see things more clearly.

Third, asking multiple people forces a person to explain their situation again and again, and that repetition sharpens their own thinking. Suppose a man is deciding whether to buy a used car from a private seller. The first time he describes the deal to a friend, he might skip over the high mileage. By the third conversation, after someone asks about it, he realizes it is the main thing bothering him. The advice matters, but so does the act of telling the story. Each conversation reveals a question he had not thought to ask.

Of course, gathering opinions can go too far. Someone who asks twenty people may end up more confused than when they started, and in the end the decision still belongs to them. The goal is not to hand the choice to a crowd. It is to collect enough perspectives that the final decision is informed instead of rushed.

Seeking multiple opinions helps people make better choices because it fills gaps in their knowledge, protects them from one-sided pressure, and clarifies what they truly care about. A good decision rarely comes from one voice. It usually comes from listening to several and then thinking carefully about what they all said.
